meta.titre: Temperature Regulation in Mammals: Keeping the Body Steady
meta.sous_theme: How the brain and skin control body temperature

sections.contenu_markdown: At midday in Limbe, a footballer sprints across the pitch. His face turns red and sweat runs down his back. At night in the highlands of Bamenda, the same boy shivers in the cold air and pulls on a sweater. In both cases the body is working to hold its temperature steady. Questions on this topic appear regularly in the GCE, usually as a request to explain the actions of the skin when the body is too hot or too cold.

items: Enzymes work best at a particular temperature.
Evaporation of a liquid takes heat from the surface it leaves.
Blood flows through arteries, capillaries and veins, and arterioles are small arteries.

sections.titre: How the body holds its temperature steady
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Why a steady temperature matters
Mammals are warm-blooded: they keep their core temperature nearly constant, about 37°C in humans, when the surroundings change. The enzymes of the body work best at this temperature. Keeping conditions inside the body steady is called **homeostasis**.

### Who is in control
The **hypothalamus**, in the brain, monitors the temperature of the blood passing through it. It also receives impulses from temperature receptors in the skin. It then sends impulses to the skin and to the muscles, which carry out the changes.

### The responses of the skin
| Part | When the body is too hot | When the body is too cold |
|---|---|---|
| Arterioles in the skin | Widen (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost | Narrow (vasoconstriction), so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost |
| Sweat glands | Make more sweat. Its evaporation takes heat from the skin | Make little or no sweat |
| Hairs | Erector muscles relax and the hairs lie flat, trapping little air | Erector muscles contract and the hairs stand up, trapping a thick layer of air |
| Muscles and metabolic rate | Metabolic rate is not raised | Muscles contract rapidly (shivering), releasing heat, and metabolic rate rises |

Trapped air is a poor conductor of heat, so a layer of it works as insulation. The blood vessels themselves do not move: the arterioles change width.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks how the skin or body copes with overheating
variantes.contenu_markdown: Make each point as a change plus its effect. Arterioles widen, so more blood reaches the surface and heat is lost by radiation. Sweat glands release sweat, and its evaporation cools the skin. Hairs lie flat, so little air is trapped and heat escapes easily. Add that the hypothalamus detects the rise.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the surroundings are cold or the question mentions shivering
variantes.contenu_markdown: Arterioles narrow, sweating stops, hairs stand up to trap insulating air, and shivering produces heat. The layer of fat under the skin also insulates the body at all times.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question mentions humid air, wind or behaviour
variantes.contenu_markdown: Sweat cools only if it evaporates. In very humid air it evaporates slowly, so cooling is poor. Behaviour helps too: resting in the shade or wearing light clothing in the heat, and wearing warm clothing in the cold.

sections.enonce_markdown: A mammal moves from a warm room into cool night air. Describe the changes that keep its body temperature steady.

etapes.justification: Cool air makes the body lose heat faster, so the body must reduce heat loss and gain heat.
Every answer should link the control centre to the response.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Receptors in the skin and the hypothalamus detect the fall and send impulses.
Arterioles in the skin narrow, so less blood flows near the surface. Sweating stops. Erector muscles contract and the hairs stand up, trapping air.

etapes.justification: Muscle activity releases heat from respiration.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Muscles shiver and metabolic rate rises.

etapes.justification: This closes the loop of control.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Less heat is lost, more heat is made, and the temperature returns to normal.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** The hypothalamus detects the fall in temperature and sends impulses to the skin and muscles. The arterioles in the skin narrow, so less blood reaches the surface and less heat is lost. Sweating stops. The hairs are pulled upright and trap a layer of air, which insulates the body. The muscles shiver and release heat, and the metabolic rate rises. Together these changes bring the temperature back to normal.

items.erreur_markdown: Blood vessels move closer to the skin surface when the body is hot.
items.pourquoi_faux: Blood vessels do not move. Only the width of the arterioles changes.
items.correction_markdown: When the body is hot the arterioles widen, so more blood flows through the skin and more heat is lost.

items.erreur_markdown: Sweating cools the body because sweat is a cold liquid.
items.pourquoi_faux: Sweat leaves the body at body temperature. The cooling comes from the change of state.
items.correction_markdown: Sweat takes heat from the skin as it evaporates, and that cools the body.

items.erreur_markdown: In the cold, hairs stand up so that heat can escape.
items.pourquoi_faux: Standing hairs trap air, which insulates the body and so reduces heat loss.
items.correction_markdown: In the cold the erector muscles contract, the hairs stand up and a thick layer of trapped air reduces heat loss.

items.erreur_markdown: The skin alone controls body temperature.
items.pourquoi_faux: The skin carries out the response. The hypothalamus in the brain detects the change and sends the instructions.
items.correction_markdown: The hypothalamus is the control centre, and the skin and muscles are the parts that respond.

items.enonce_markdown: For each response, say whether it occurs when the body is too hot or too cold: (a) the arterioles in the skin narrow, (b) sweat production rises, (c) the muscles shiver, (d) the hairs lie flat.
A boy runs hard around a field. His face turns red and he sweats heavily. Explain both observations.
items.solution_markdown: Running makes the muscles respire faster and release a lot of heat, so the body is overheating. The arterioles in the skin widen, and the extra blood flowing near the surface makes the face look **red**. This increases heat loss. The sweat glands make **sweat**, and its evaporation takes heat from the skin and cools the body.

items.enonce_markdown: Two people do the same exercise on a hot day. One is in dry air and the other in very humid air. Both sweat heavily, but the person in humid air stays much hotter and feels more uncomfortable. Explain why.
items.solution_markdown: Sweat cools the body only when it evaporates. Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so sweat **evaporates slowly** there. Little heat is taken from the skin, and the sweat just runs off or stays on the skin. The person in dry air loses heat quickly as the sweat evaporates, so the temperature falls back to normal. The person in humid air keeps the extra heat for longer, so the body stays hotter.

items_markdown: The hypothalamus is the control centre for body temperature, and the skin and muscles carry out the response.
When too hot: the arterioles widen, sweat is made and the hairs lie flat.
When too cold: the arterioles narrow, sweating stops, the hairs stand up and the muscles shiver.
Trapped air is a poor conductor of heat, so it insulates.
Sweat cools only by evaporating, and the arterioles change width without the vessels moving.
